speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO NUMBER OP SECRET ORDERS STILL IN EFFECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last I answered orally question No. 326 asked by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) concerning orders in council passed since January 1, 1955. Later on the orders of the day the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked me whether I could say if any, and if so how many, secret orders in council passed prior to January 1, 1955, are still in effect.
I stated then that I would take the question as notice, because I did not remember that there were any and that I would have a check made. I have had that check made and I wish to say that there are none in effect at the present time. The one I referred to in the house on March 26, 1953, depended for its validity upon the Emergency Powers Act; and when that act expired the order in council ceased to have any force or effect.

maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO NUMBER OP SECRET ORDERS STILL IN EFFECT
speechtext:
May
I ask a supplementary question? How many orders are there that have not been published and what is the difference between an order in council that is not available for publication and a secret order in council? What is the distinction between them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO NUMBER OP SECRET ORDERS STILL IN EFFECT
speechtext:
Orders in council that are published are those that are required to be so published under the Regulations Act. The others are summarized and the summary is tabled, I think it is each
month. If any order that is not published is asked for and is not a secret order, it is available to those who ask for it. The publishing of all the orders in council and all the treasury board minutes would, I believe, be a very voluminous and costly undertaking. I think it was on the hon. member's suggestion that this summary of orders in council was made available, and that has always been made available.
I do not know of any question that has arisen about any order. I explained, in answer to the hon. gentleman's question, that there were some orders which we felt, in delicacy to other countries whose affairs were concerned, it was preferable not to make public but arrangements could be made to allow them to be seen confidentially by any hon. member who was interested.

maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO NUMBER OP SECRET ORDERS STILL IN EFFECT
speechtext: It was of those I was inquiring. I am not asking for publication of all and I know what the arrangement was. How many are there of those orders in council to which the minister referred at the end of his last statement? How many are there that, because of their delicate nature or because of their relationship with other countries, are not publicly available and are only available confidentially to those members who ask for them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO NUMBER OP SECRET ORDERS STILL IN EFFECT
speechtext: I believe I would have to make a personal examination of the orders to ascertain that. We endeavour to avoid any suggestion that we are trying to keep any orders in council secret, so if any order is asked for and if the officials find it would come within that category, they would probably mention it to me and I would try to make it available if it were at all possible to do so without creating suggestions of discourtesy to other governments.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF CERTIFICATION OF UNIONS
speechtext:
I promised to answer this week a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The question was as to whether steps will be taken for the continuation of all certifications under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, regardless of changes of union name that may result from the merger of the two congresses. While some aspects of this matter are still under consideration by my department, I can make the following reply.
If all that is involved is a change in name arising out of the merger, and no change in the union entity is involved, it is considered that this matter of a change of name can be dealt with without difficulty under the existing provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act by application of the interested union to the labour relations board for an amendment of the order of certification.
There is, however, a further question which arises as to the status of local unions directly chartered by either of the two labour congresses which have been certified as bargaining agents under our act.
It is planned, I understand, by the new congresses to have new charters issued by the new congress to these congress chartered local unions. The question has been raised as to whether the procedure which the new congress proposes to follow will have the effect of extinguishing the entity of the original union and the establishment of a new union in place thereof, or whether the entity of the old union will be preserved under a new name. This is the point which is still getting consideration.
However, my officials advise me that this matter raises no problem of any consequence under our federal act as there are only 15 of these congress chartered unions which have been certified under the federal legislation. The view of my officials at this time is that this matter is not one which will require legislation, but I will report on this point later.


I should add that this situation raises a larger and more serious problem in the case of some of the provincial boards where many certifications have been issued to such unions.

Mr. Chairman, when the consideration of public works estimates ended on Friday last we were dealing with this particular item, and I pointed out to the minister that while the vote this year is $900,000, the details found at page 469 indicate that during the fiscal year which expired on March 31 the sum of only $350,000 had been spent. That seemed to be a rather strange procedure. I am wondering if it would not be possible to cut down this vote for the present year.
I would point out to the committee that the public works estimates contain other votes of a similar nature designed to give the minister a source from which he may draw if there should be unforeseen expenditures required. For example, one such vote is vote No. 391 which reads:
To supplement, on approval of treasury board except where less than $1,000 is required, any of the appropriations of the Department of Public Works, $750,000.
It will be noted that that particular vote is $350,000 more than it was last year. With provisions such as that in the estimates for unforeseen contingencies surely there is no need to ask for such a large amount under item 364.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
I spoke briefly to this item just before we concluded our study of the estimates last Friday. This vote is required to cover works of a structural nature for which there is no specific appropriation but which cannot be charged to the maintenance votes under the allotment "Repairs and Upkeep'', such as installation of new elevators, ventilating systems, construction of small additions, fire escapes, etc. and major repairs such as strengthening foundations, support walls or floors and construction of roofs. Those are items that cannot be specifically foreseen when the estimates are prepared.

On February 20 Captain Dale-Johnson was suspended from his duties. On the same date the Department of Transport was requested to carry out a preliminary investigation. This investigation found that the Hilunga was properly manned and equipped at the time of the accident and that even with the wind increased to 50 miles per hour she behaved well. The inquiry found that the stranding was caused by an extraordinary leeward drift due to a wind of gale force acting on the high superstructure. The incident was, in fact, a grim reminder of the rapidity with which weather conditions can change on that part of the coast. In this particular case it took only four or five hours for a quiet, pleasant passage to change to the difficulties of a howling gale in low visibility. The weather experienced was in accordance with warnings issued by the meteorological service but the change took place somewhat sooner than the forecast predicted. The master set his course at a distance from shore which he considered ample to take care of any drift but in this he was mistaken. In the falling snow with radar ineffective in such a sea, the first indication the crew had that she was too near shore came when they felt a bump as though a log had been struck.
The investigation also revealed that this accident was a straight case of an error in judgment on the part of the master of the vessel in deciding to go outside the coastal islands instead of following the long and tortuous inside passage to Prince Rupert and across the eastern shore of the Queen Charlotte islands.

Now, I think that I might report on the situation with regard to Port aux Basques, Newfoundland. As hon. members know, we have been engaged at the request of the Department of Transport in considering and implementing improvements to this harbour to prepare it for its role under the terms of confederation as the Newfoundland terminus for the Canadian National Railways vessel William Carson.
In this connection the Department of Transport engaged the services of Messrs. Coode and Partners, British consulting engineers, last year. As a result of their report which was made last August 15, coupled with our own judgment, the government decided to implement at once a two-point program. The first of these consisted of the construction of a breakwater approximately 600 feet in length which would extend from Graveyard Point to West Baldwin Rock. A contract for this work was awarded on December 9, 1955 to Tidewater Construction Company Limited, New Glasgow, N.S., at unit prices totalling approximately $186,600. This work is well under way and is approximately 35 per cent completed. It is expected that the breakwater will be finished by July 1.
The second decision was to have the national research council construct and conduct studies on a hydraulic scale model of the harbour at an estimated cost of $70,000. This model will be operated by personnel of the national research council and the Department of Public Works. Our aim in erecting it is to study whether the harbour [DOT]will be satisfactory with the addition of the new breakwater or whether further improvements may be necessary. I can report that a necessary extension to the hydraulic laboratory of the national research council to house this new model has been finished and that the model itself has been completed.
Preliminary studies and the collection of additional information at Port aux Basques itself have also been finished. The final adjustment now has been made to the machine which will simulate waves. It is


estimated that the model tests will start in early May and that some results will be available sometime this summer. Once these studies have been made we will be in a better position to judge the situation with regard to Port aux Basques.

The inside passage is in the nature of a series of canals right up direct to Prince Rupert. Those canals are well within the mainland. They are not right out on the open ocean; they are well inside. That is the way the passenger vessels go to Prince Rupert. It is a marvellous natural canal route. It is what is known on the west coast as the inside passage. Apparently this little ship was never ordered to go around through the inside passage. The way she had to go was off the main shore, that is, right through the Hecate strait. The distance from Triple island to Rose Spit at the northern end of the

speechtext: I think the responsibilities of a captain on his own ship are obvious. I shall be glad to do that, Mr. Chairman. This is exactly the situation as the minister has outlined it. For the last 40 years various firms have been using the Sturgeon river for floating their logs down into lake Nipissing. At the present time, as in the past, some of the companies are co-operating and doing this in a way that will cause the least inconvenience to the public and to the tourist resort operators along that important river.
Now, sometimes as I say there is cooperation and intelligence used, and sometimes there is not. Sometimes there is a complete disregard for the navigation interests of the river. There always seems to be a problem, and this has continued for 40 years. Members of parliament, the chamber of commerce, the mayors, the town councils, all seem to be running around in circles on this particular problem. Usually, of course, it ends up with a member of parliament who makes representations to the minister. The minister then goes to his engineers and the engineers go out, but by that time either nature or the company concerned has taken care of the problem and so another year goes by.
I should like to know just what teeth there may be in this Navigable Waters Protection Act. I have looked it up this morning and in the interpretation section under "work" we find this:
"Work" includes any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock . . .
And so on. Then it goes on to say that it includes any structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not, which may interfere with navigation.

Then later on under the heading "General" we find this:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water-
Then it goes on to mention any other thing by which any obstruction or obstacle is caused. Now, it seems to me that is fairly complete. While it is true that this act is the responsibility of another minister, the Minister of Transport-

I should like to have this problem solved for the people of my area. It is a very real problem. We are dependent to a great degree on the tourist dollars that are spent in the area. Last year we had a situation where two firms used the river for the purposes I mentioned earlier. One of them did it in a way that was indeed commendable. They avoided week ends, holidays and so on and their logs were moved down the river with the very least inconvenience to the people who were using the river for boating purposes, the transportation of tourist supplies and tourists. In so far as the other firm was concerned the contrary was true. I stepped into the thing, perhaps needlessly or improperly, but I was quite concerned. The other company listened and assured us that the same co-operation would be forthcoming, but that has never transpired.
Now, I do not want to let this continue. I want to approach this problem in an honest way. If we have any responsibility, if there are any teeth in the legislation, I want the provisions of it carried out and the problem settled. There is no point in allowing it to continue for another 40 years. If we have no authority, if we have no jurisdiction, if there are no teeth in the legislation, let us be honest and say so. I would appreciate hearing any comments the minister can make about the problem because it is a needless and annoying one. It arises from the careless disregard of one organization. I do not say that in any unkind sense and I do not know the principals of that organization at all. But if there are any teeth in the legislation it should be implemented so that the tourist

operators and the people who use the Sturgeon river will not have this sort of problem in the future.

Mr. Chairman, item 365 of the estimates of the Department of Public Works, dealing with harbours and rivers, gives me an excellent opportunity of again asking the government to be kind enough to undertake, with the least possible delay, works which have been requested long ago by myself in the house on several occasions, as well as by the Quebec municipal council, the Chamber of Commerce and all the important public bodies of the old capital.
I want to refer once again to those two rivers which have been mentioned so often previously in this house, so often in fact that at times it seemed that we could detect their smell, rivers which need to be cleansed and deepened or canalized with the least possible delay and for many reasons. But, Mr. Chairman, even though there would be only one reason, that is to safeguard public health, I believe it would be very important since public health is our most precious asset in Canada.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that there is at present and that there has been for some time a conflict of jurisdiction as far as the responsibility for those two rivers, located in the city of Quebec, is concerned. Here in the parliament of the nation, the federal government contends that it is a provincial responsibility, while elsewhere the contrary is upheld. Some people go so far as to say that it is a matter that concerns the municipal authorities. I do not intend to argue that point. However, there seems to be a conflict and nothing seems to have been done to define the jurisdiction in any concrete way. People are still mixed up on the matter, but one thing remains, Mr. Chairman, and that is that the health of the people of Quebec is constantly endangered.
I have often mentioned in the house the foul smells which cover the whole city and constitute a grave danger. I want to emphasize again here that between these two rivers, in the heart of the city of Quebec, the most important playground has been laid out, where underprivileged children, whose parents cannot afford to spend the summer outside the city, can enjoy themselves and where, I readily admit, they are sheltered from the dangers of traffic. But, unquestion-67509-198
Supply-Public Works
ably, they are exposed to perhaps an even greater danger, that of infection from some virus emanating from these open sewers, and which could impair their health for the rest of their lives.
This seems to be a very important point, and I urge the government, on the eve of general elections, to act on a kindly impulse. I do not ask them to settle this whole problem this year or next. However, I do ask them to show their willingness to take the necessary and urgent steps required to put an end to this situation which has existed in the city of Quebec for more than a quarter of a century and which, unfortunately, has never been corrected.
Mr. Chairman, the municipal council of the City of Quebec-this is for the information of the hon. members of this house-has decided, at the end of last month I believe, to spend $350,000 for the diversion and improvement of a part of St. Charles river. There would be no point in trying to conceal the fact that the Quebec municipal authorities are aware of the necessity of such a move, to protect the citizens of Quebec. Needless to say, the city of Quebec surely lacks the means to finance such an undertaking. Where will she get the money? It is not for me to discuss the point but we all know that the city of Quebec is at present in financial difficulties and that this new burden would inevitably fall on the shoulders of the Quebec taxpayers who, I think, are already overtaxed.
As I was saying a moment ago, I wonder if some means could not be found, on the eve of an impending election, to include a substantial vote towards the sanitation and deepening work which appears to be necessary in the case of the St. Charles river, a river which at all events, comes under federal jurisdiction.
I would very much like the city of Quebec to be as attractive as Ottawa is at this time, when we look at the splendid Rideau canal which cuts across this capital city.
The St. Charles and Lairet rivers are little better than sewers, as I have already pointed out. They are a disgrace to the capital of my province. I would hope that serious consideration will be given to correcting this state of affairs, apart altogether from the matter of jurisdiction which, in any case, has not been settled yet.
Should the federal government decide to offer a substantial grant so that this work

Supply-Public Works
could begin-which would be a fine gesture on its part-who knows but that other authorities would not be ready to follow its lead?
The city of Quebec has, on its part, shown a willingness which could properly be called remarkable, and the ratepayers of Quebec would be only too happy, I should think, to welcome such a step on the part of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), and especially of his parliamentary assistant (Mr. Bourget) who probably knows more about this matter, in fact, that anyone here.
It is not a case of blaming anybody in particular for the fact that this situation has not been remedied yet. Let us forget about the past, let us only look to the present and, especially, let us look to the future and the health of our children, especially those of the city of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, having dealt with this matter, I would now like to speak about one which has already been raised in this house two years ago, I believe. It has to do with the award of certain contracts.
Contracts have been awarded to companies of questionable solvency. I have reference in this regard to a contract of close to $500,000 awarded for the widening of the wharf at Riviere du Loup, in the constituency of Temiscouata. Mr. Chairman, let me at once reassure the hon. members sitting opposite; this is no personal attack against anyone in this house. Neither the Minister of Public Works, nor his parliamentary assistant, no more than the present member for Temiscouata (Mr. St. Laurent), is to be blamed for that situation. I want to be fair to everyone.
A contract for the widening of the wharf at Riviere du Loup was awarded to a Canadian company, the subsidiary of a British company operating under the name of Marples Ridgway Canada Limited. The work was completed last year. It is not a bad thing that this happened a little before the by-election in that constituency, but that was probably mere coincidence. As I was saying, the work was completed, it was approved by the federal government engineers, and what happened then? Unfortunately, I repeat, unfortunately, on December 3 last, the newly constructed section collapsed by some 15 feet, so that it was necessary to condemn the wharf. Federal government engineers were rushed to the spot and I believe they have been there ever since, if not permanently, at least periodically, to make the soundings
[Mr. Dufresne.l
required to determine how the works could be repaired. However, what is even more unfortunate is that, two days after the collapse of that new part of the wharf, the company which had been awarded the contract, also collapsed in a spectacular bankruptcy amounting to $638,320.61, causing the loss of considerable sums of money all across the country and also in the area concerned, i.e. the Riviere du Loup area.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the committee rose at one o'clock, I was saying that the Marples Ridgway Canada Company Limited, which had built

or, at any rate, widened the wharf at Riviere du Loup, collapsed two days after the wharf itself had done so, in a $638,320.61 bankruptcy.
Mr. Chairman, the suggestion I would make today is to recommend to the government that all contracts be at least awarded to responsible firms. Some might say that the department has no knowledge of the solvency of the company which secures a contract. But it seems to me that inquiries should be made to find out if a company being awarded a contract can fulfil it without causing many people, subcontractors and even workers, to lose large amounts of money they cannot afford to lose.
Here we have a situation where the Canadian people, because the government failed to take necessary precautions, will lose close to a million dollars, not to mention the extra work of the engineers who have been making soundings since last fall. And that is not all, for the new construction will probably cost as much as the amount which has already been lost, that is about half a million dollars. Therefore the widening of that wharf will cost a pretty penny, over a million dollars whereas, with a little more foresight, it would probably have been possible to save $500,000.
As I said at the outset, I am not blaming anybody at this time. I am only mentioning these things as I think it is my duty to bring them to the attention of the committee. The same thing happened two years ago, and I remember there was quite a discussion in this house at the time. It seemed somewhat

identical, and I would not like it to occur again, if possible.
In addition to this loss of more than a million dollars incurred by the government, the Department of National Revenue lost a further amount of $6,000 after deductions; the provincial treasury experienced a loss of about $15,000; and what seems to me somewhat difficult to understand, Mr. Chairman, is that the company that went bankrupt two days after the collapse of the widened wharf left a considerable list of creditors. I have the list here. It contains five full pages of people claiming the amount just mentioned. Moreover, what seems to me unaccountable is that, according to my information, last year this company obtained contracts for about a million dollars from the government of Newfoundland, and for many hundred thousand dollars in the province of Ontario. This seems to jibe, for most of the creditors on the list are from Newfoundland and Ontario.
I know some of the people in the Riviere du Loup district, Mr. Chairman, who certainly cannot afford to lose the money due to them. I have been told that the subcontractors have sent in their statements to the department. Unfortunately, I understand the government's policy, and I know that the government has no responsibility as regards subcontractors, but only to the main contractor. However, I am stressing the fact that steps should be taken to ascertain the solvency of companies to which quite imposing contracts are being awarded by the Department of Public Works.
There is also another point upon which I want to draw the attention of this house. The company to which I referred did not start to operate in Canada before November 1951, and its incorporation, according to the information I obtained from the Secretary of State, dates from February, 1954. It is, therefore, obvious that when the company was awarded the contract for a wharf at Riviere du Loup, it was already in financial straits. It shows how important it is for the government to enquire into the solvency of firms to which contracts are awarded.
I hope, for the benefit of the working people of the district, that they will be able to resume work as soon as possible, and that the government will make it' possible for those subcontractors to recover some of their losses.
I have only one more word to add, Mr. Chairman. I see from this year's estimates that a considerable amount of money is being 67509-198$

I am going to consolidate my few remarks in order to save the time of the house. I

want to say a word or two about the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I understand this act has been on the statute books for many years and that there are two departments that have responsibility for administering the act: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. Judging, from my experience and observations in recent years, the act needs a thorough overhauling because changed circumstances and developments have created new problems. I find on some occasions there is some doubt as to the jurisdiction of the various departments.
I understand that the Department of Public Works builds the wharves and then hands them over to the Department of Transport to administer them; but under certain circumstances such as those existing in a number of places in my constituency I do not think the present procedures are satisfactory. That is why I suggest that there should be an overhauling of the act. I know it is not possible for the Department of Transport to have sufficient representatives to oversee the damage to all wharves at all times. On that account there are violations of the law, and sometimes there is damage to wharves that is not reported for some time. I can think of wharves at the present time as to which, if the damage had been reported as soon as it occurred, the cost of repair would have been considerably lessened.
That is why I suggest there should be some change in procedure. I suggest that in isolated districts it would be wise to make some provision for the R.C.M.P. to supervise and keep an eye on wharves and public facilities of that sort, and that in other more isolated districts it might be wise to get the postmaster to report to the Department of Transport. I think that sort of thing is required.
I have one other suggestion to make with respect to the Navigable Waters Protection Act. From my personal observation the section of the act that has to do with pollution of navigable waters by sawdust, slabs and things of that sort has not been enforced throughout the years. That was not a serious problem when we had only a small amount of industry in the district, but I think those sections of the act should now be enforced. Even in recent years I have seen large areas of our lakes covered with a coating of sawdust that has been dumped in the lake by sawmills; and in recent years I have seen large areas of the lake covered with slabs which are a hazard to navigation, particularly to small boats.
Supply-Public Works
I suggest that some consideration should be given to co-operating with the provincial game department of British Columbia. The provincial game department have tried their best throughout the years to enforce the provincial laws having to do with the pollution of waters, particularly pollution by sawdust, slabs and things of that sort. So far as the Department of Transport is concerned, I think it has been completely dormant. With the great increase in industry and therefore the greater damage that might be done to our fish and the greater hazard to navigation, particularly to small boats, I suggest that this section of the Navigable Waters Protection Act should possibly be revised and that arrangements should be made to see that it is enforced to the public good and common advantage.

While we are on this item 365 relating to the general administration of harbours across the nation, there are a few remarks I should like to make about the policy of administering the expenditure of money in a particular area, namely in the Toronto harbour area. In talking of the Toronto harbour commission and about harbours generally I realize that there is a certain amount of overlapping as between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. What I have to say will, I think, be of interest to the minister, and perhaps the suggestions I have to make may in time bear some fruit.
We have in the city of Toronto a harbour commission which administers the expenditure of money from the department. I think this year we have some $300,000 in the estimates for the Toronto harbour commission. It is composed of five members, one of whom is appointed by the federal government. The Toronto harbour commission has, as I say, responsibility for the works in the Toronto harbour, but they are strictly confined to Toronto city. As all hon. members know, we now have superimposed over the whole of Toronto metropolitan area an organization known as the metropolitan Toronto corporation. Its responsibilities cover all aspects of existence and life in the metropolitan Toronto area, including transport and allied matters. At the same time the Toronto harbour commission which administers the funds provided by the Department of Public Works still has within its jurisdiction only the now narrow confines of the city proper, the old city of Toronto.

Supply-Public Works
The area, as we know, contains about 1-| million people-that is the metropolitan area -and it has a vast potential in so far as its extension and expansion is concerned. The lake front, for example, of the metropolitan area is some 28 miles in length, only a small part of which covers the actual city of Toronto area. It has been my view for some time now that the harbour commission's power should be extended to cover the whole 28 miles of lake frontage. In other words I feel that we should have a metropolitan Toronto harbours commission.
My reasons are as follows. First, we can expect a great increase and development in the use of the metropolitan Toronto lake front. I know the expansion we expect through the St. Lawrence seaway will not have a terrific impact on all 28 miles of lake front, but my point is that if we are going to develop that harbour properly, if we are going to take full advantage of any expansion that might come about, then the Toronto harbour commission should at least have jurisdiction to look at and examine the whole 28 miles of lake front area-because there is no telling just what might be done best to develop that area-rather than be confined merely to the narrow city bounds.
For example, we have heard many rumours -whether or not there is anything in them I do not know-that the area around Port Union which happens to lie in my constituency provides somewhat better natural harbour facilities than does the city of Toronto harbour. It might well be that the Toronto harbour commission should be looking at that as an alternative to spending more money on developing to a greater extent the harbour that we have at present. In my opinion, Toronto harbour is not a particularly good natural harbour.
There are other navigational difficulties which face the Department of Public Works and which dictate a broader scope for the harbour commission. That is my second point. I am thinking of the dredging work they carry on. A great part of this $300,000 which we will see later in the estimates is for dredging work that has to be carried out annually in the Toronto harbour. Each year silt is deposited in a particular part of the harbour called the eastern gap, which is an important entrance to the harbour. That requires the constant expenditure of money to keep it clear for shipping. I remember that Professor Griffiths Taylor, a rather famous geographer at the University of Toronto, had a favourite theory based on what

I think were good grounds, namely that the silt that plugged up the eastern gap was carved by the lake currents from Scarborough Bluffs.
You will see now, Mr. Chairman, that I am getting down to a rather selfish part of my representation. It can easily be argued, Mr. Chairman, that the silt from Scarborough Bluffs which is taken by those currents and dropped off in eastern gap, thus creating a difficult situation in Scarborough, is part and parcel of the same problem. We in Scarborough have been making representations for many years now to the effect that the federal government should assist in doing something to help stop the erosion of Scarborough Bluffs, and at great risk I again raise the question in this connection.

I believe, however, that on my explanation, we can find good legal grounds for bringing it within the jurisdiction of the federal government by relating it to the expense of maintaining the harbour of the city of Toronto.
I believe there are several spheres of activity of the Department of Public Works, for example along the St. Lawrence river, where they built retaining walls to stop the banks from caving in, which would justify my submission. The department justifies this work on the basis of assistance to navigation and the fact it is necessary to maintain good navigational conditions in the river. I believe that on that basis we can make a good case to bring the problem of Scarborough bluffs also within the jurisdiction of the federal government. It is that point I want to make for the minister's consideration.
There has been some concrete work done on this problem. The residents, in cooperation with the township of Scarborough, have built what they call groynes which extend out into the water and help stabilize the shore line. The groynes go out some 50

to 60 feet into the water and are about one and a half feet wide at the top, in the shape of an inverted T. They are not very expensive. I think the cost of installing one groyne is approximately $6,000. Actually, if we had about 10 or 15 groynes constructed at the present time, it would go a long way towards assisting in this present problem, the problem being that houses along the bluff are falling into the lake as a result of the constant erosion that is taking place.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that outlines the problem as far as I can at this time. I think it would be interesting to hear from the metropolitan Toronto corporation itself as to its attitude towards the extension of the Toronto harbour commission to cover the whole of the metropolitan area. I believe it is as certain as I am standing here that if we do not look ahead and take cognizance of the problem that will arise in the future development of this area, and take steps to organize and prepare for it now in an effort to take full advantage of the potential development, we are going to regret it.

I believe the minister knows what I have in mind so I shall be as brief as I can. Within about 10 miles of Sarnia, in fact near my own place, Mr. Chairman, we have what is really a river. In the summer it plugs up with about five or six feet of sand. Going back a few years the departmental engineer in London had pictures taken of the mouth of the river showing the quantity of sand which prevented the flow of the water into the lake. This resulted in the water backing up and flooding the land. As a matter of fact at that particular time it was necessary for the farmers who grew sugar beets to ship by rail instead of by truck because of the nematode disease. The truck method of shipment would be apt to spread the nematodes to other areas. I quite appreciate the minister's attitude because, after all is said and done, he must interpret the act as it is 67509-199
Supply-Public Works
drawn, with all its various amendments, and for that reason I am suggesting a change.
Some time last year the township council started a project of building groynes on either side of this river projecting into the lake in order to stop erosion and make a harbour for fishing boats and other craft, including tourist boats. I might say that never before in this house have I asked for one penny that was not for a self-liquidating project.
I do not think it is fair for any member in the house to ask that money be spent here and there, because after all it is the taxpayers' money. If the time comes when the labour situation becomes worse, I know there will be a flood of public works by the provinces, the municipalities and the federal government in an endeavour to take up the slack.
Now, this would be a self-liquidating project. Inasmuch as the council has already started the work, I understand from the minister that he cannot give a permit to complete the work. I think, as I have explained to the minister, the council would like a permit in order to get some financial assistance. I am going to be frank about that. Without a permit they cannot get it. If the act is so rigid, and so ancient there is no leeway in a matter that does not involve a principle to any great extent and which would afford a great deal of relief to those people who live along the shore, including the fishermen, then I hope the minister's advisers will consider an immediate revision of the act. In the past people who have started such projects have somehow or other obtained permits. In many cases they did not even get permits, but if they wanted to get provincial assistance I think it was necessary for them to get a federal permit and comply with the act.
Now this Navigable Waters Protection Act is a federal matter, and we are concerned about it. We are concerned that the procedure be legal. There are other groynes along the lake. If the project could be completed it would afford the fishermen along there a measure of protection. God knows they are hard enough up today owing to the lamprey menace. If the project could be completed some of the fishermen could find refuge in this particular area for their fishing craft. That in itself is something worth while.
With respect to the other matter I mentioned a minute ago, we are not very far from

Detroit. As I said earlier, it would be a self-liquidating project. The first is the question of the breakwater that was built at White Rock in 1953. Undoubtedly that breakwater had a purpose when it was built. I am satisfied that the people in the White Rock area are wondering now what that particular purpose was, because apparently it is not doing the job it was intended to do. For instance, I have the report of the board of trade of White Rock. It is not too long, but I do not intend to read all of it. It reads in part:
The following list comprises owners of boats that would anchor at White Rock if suitable protection was available. The boats are now anchored at Blaine, Washington, New Westminster and Vancouver.
The list consists of some 40-odd names, some of which the minister and one of which the committee will recognize. The report closes with these two sentences:
The Semiahmoo yacht club of 150 members has approximately 40 boats under construction or on order from manufacturers.
This is over and above some 50 or 60 boats and owners that are listed. I continue with the quotation:
During , a storm in October, 1954, five craft that were moored behind the breakwater were severely damaged due to the inadequate protection and two boats tied to the float had to be moved as water was too rough.
The report is signed by L. Young and O. Matt. It does seem to me that a breakwater which cost us well over $100,000, as I understand it, was intended to give boats that would moor behind it some measure of protection. I am not blaming the minister, but possibly sufficient foresight was not taken. Was it the intention to follow up this particular structure by adding more to it or do some other engineering work within the region to afford the boat owners the protection they have the right to expect? It does seem to me most unfortunate that they have to moor their boats at Blaine, Washington, at New Westminster and at Vancouver harbour, particularly in view of the fact that the locality concerned is a summer resort, and many people like to leave their boats there during the summer months and in the fall season as well, and use them whenever they are needed.
I should like the minister to comment on this question and outline to the satisfaction of myself and the community the intention of the department with respect to this particular breakwater. Is it the intention to leave it as is and say, "Well, we put so many thousand dollars down the drain"? Is it the intention to carry on and do something specific with it? What are the plans? I do not think sufficient thought was given at the time

the breakwater was put in to warrant the expenditure at that time unless something further was intended.
I have two other questions that relate to another locality. I mentioned one on an earlier occasion. I refer to the protection required by those who own homes in the Beach Grove area along Boundary bay. The wind and the tide come sweeping across the bay and, in the winter months particularly, wreak a great deal of havoc on the homeowners in that locality. Mr. Chairman, after my three false starts I was beginning to think there were several other ridings that must have in them some of the bluffs to which the hon. member for Scarborough referred.

Supply-Public Works
As a matter of fact, Mr, Chairman, I had not thought it possible to speak on this item in the terms in which the hon. member for Scarborough spoke. Perhaps he used a bluffing system on the minister in connection with his remarks. It occurs to me, too, that perhaps I may be excused if I deal with the same subject at this time.
Throughout the whole Toronto area we are very much interested at the present time in any plans for development which are going to assist in providing the best inland port that can be found anywhere on the North American continent. I think a word of congratulation might be due to the administration of the Toronto harbour commission for the work that is being carried on there at the present time. I have referred on other occasions to the fact that a great deal of vision is going to be required in this matter or we are not going to keep pace with the development of the shipping which is going to go through the new seaway. We are vitally interested in that. Unless the facilities for handling cargo is improved we are of course going to lose business to other ports.
I say that, sir, because we have a wonderful natural harbour, but I think to a certain extent we are restricted in the dock area we have on the mainland side. I think we will have to look to the future. Although many residents of what is known as our island area would consider it unfortunate if the character of that area were changed, if Toronto is going to develop to its true potential as a result of the seaway it may be necessary for the dockage area to be extended there, too.
While I am on that point I might say that we have heard a lot about the use of the tunnel to the island. I know that the minister will probably say that that is a matter for the Department of Transport and it does not come under his department, but if proper provision is going to be made for the facilities we require then I think the Department of Public Works in liaison with the Department of Transport might go back to the old records somewhere around the year 1911 and look up an undertaking which was given concerning the provision of federal funds for that project. It may be vitally important to the development of that area.
There is one other vital concern at the present time. The metropolitan area of Toronto is a new creation. It is experiencing great difficulty in carrying out all its necessary expansion features. I feel that there may be a slight note of difference of opinion creeping in concerning the administration of

the harbour area. I think this is of tremendous importance to the department, because it is spending money to provide dockage facilities.
As I say, there is a slight difference of opinion creeping in, in connection with the administration and the wishes of the metropolitan Toronto area. There is some very valuable property there which if it is not administered in the proper manner may become a blighted area. I think the value of the money that is being put into docks there may be seriously depreciated thereby. I am thinking about the proposed plans for super highways which will run through the area. If some of the plans are approved, then I believe we may find that the area immediately adjacent to the area provided for warehouses and offices for that type of business may become similar to those which one sees in New York, and their real property value would be depreciated.
These problems arise, sir, because there are little differences of opinion in connection with other matters.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member would mind if I were to interject at this point. I am sure the hon. member means to be in order, and he probably believes he is quite in order. The actual harbour administration in Toronto is under their own statute which federally is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport. It does not come within the scope of jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works, except to the extent that I am the tradesman who builds wharves wherever I am asked, subject to appropriate approvals. I have nothing to do with the administration and operation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY

I shall be only a couple of minutes more on this. I have attempted to be just as much in order as the hon. member for York-Scarborough. I related my remarks to the fact that the minister is responsible for the spending of this money, and that if in the background there was not close liaison between the Toronto harbour commission and the Toronto metropolitan officials many hundreds of thousands of dollars may be spent without any value being obtained in return.
I shall close this phase of my remarks quickly by saying that these things come up because we may have instances where the harbour commission will license people to do certain things with land, and then there is a throwback in connection with the operation of the immediate area at the dock. The same thing may apply to other remarks I am going

to make, because here again it is an administration item and the minister may very well say that it comes under the Department of Transport.
The metropolitan council has been called upon to pay a quarter of a million dollars for protective work in connection with the harbour police and lifesaving activities in that area. Perhaps the minister will say this does not come under his department, but these things are required because certain facilities have been provided. It always comes back to the same point. I recall what the hon. member for Charlotte said, that when somebody wants to spend money you cannot economize. I always think the only way we will get true economy is to have the people who spend the money collect the money. Until we reach that point in connection with our various expenditures, municipal, provincial or federal, we will always have this situation.
I think the true responsibility is not that of the municipality. A quarter of a million dollars must be spent for this purpose by the municipality when it needs money for the building of schools and other items. This type of protection is needed for facilities provided by the federal department. Taking it from the tax source picture, there just is not a base to provide for it. Whether it is a responsibility of this department or of the Department of Transport, I submit that the time has come for a change in the method of handling these expenditures.
As far as the facilities generally are concerned, I submit that there should be better access provided to the lake. I believe one of the hon. members from a Toronto riding has a question on the order paper dealing with this. There seems to be a continual difficulty in connection with the providing of proper access and the dredging of the channels. If that comes within the jurisdiction of the minister I think he might take a look at the problem.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one or two matters I should like to bring up. I have been badgering the officials of the department about one matter and perhaps I could badger the minister a little bit more in the hope of getting some action. I refer to the breakwater at Northwest bay north of Nanaimo. The department has spent a considerable amount of money there, but I regret to say that it is money down the drain because they have not completed the job they started.
A rock fill was built, and from the end of the rock fill a log boom was placed running to the reef further out in the bay. To my knowledge that boom has had to be
Supply-Public Works
replaced twice. It becomes waterlogged and the first storm drives it out, and the whole project is then completely useless. There are a number of settlers with boats in that area. When the log boom was put in it looked as though this would be a safe harbour, and an oil company put in a float and a fish company also placed a buying float in this area. However, they have since been taken away due to the failure of the department to build a breakwater in such a way as to ensure continual protection in that little harbour.
When one looks at the east coast of Vancouver island he might think there were endless safe harbours all the way up the coast. The map seems to suggest that, but as a matter of fact they are very few and far between. After you leave Nanaimo going north there is literally no adequate small boat harbour until you get to Courtenay. There is of course the project which has been commenced at the mouth of French creek, and I see according to the estimates that something is to be done at Deep bay. But these are both in the future. I do not think the French creek project will be of any great importance to commercial fishermen.
It is the commercial fisherman whom I have in mind in connection with the Northwest bay project. I have contacted many of them, and they tell me they had hoped to use this as their seasonal base but found they could not do so. At one time they had hoped that they might be able to use Nanoose bay behind the breakwater, but unfortunately at low water the breakwater encloses only the smallest of puddles in which it would be most difficult to get more than six boats. It is mainly for the protection of the C.P.R. transfer dock for the car barge, but as a small boat harbour it just simply does not exist. I urge the minister to look into this project to see whether it would not provide a suitable site, and complete the job which was begun some years ago.
I should like now to turn to another project which has been in the air for a long time. I had hoped that after the visit of the minister to Nanaimo last year perhaps this would have been gone ahead with. I refer to the assembly dock in Nanaimo. It was perhaps unfortunate that when the minister was there only one boat happened to be at the assembly dock, but I can assure the minister that at almost all times there will be three or four deep-sea vessels lying in the stream waiting to get in to load lumber. I do think this is a project which should be proceeded with. I understand there has been some difficulty with regard to the interest of the provincial authorities, although I have not been able to get to the bottom of that in

Supply-Public Works
my correspondence with them. I should like to see some move made in this connection.
There is another matter in connection with Nanaimo harbour which I think should engage the attention of the department. I have mentioned this once or twice to the departmental officials. I realize it is a rather difficult project to take hold of. I refer to the future of what is sometimes known as Commercial inlet in Nanaimo harbour. Some time ago a commercial firm in Nanaimo began to dump rock in this area. Complaints were made about this, which I brought to the attention of the department, and for a while I believe it was stopped. Now I understand there are plans on foot to seriously consider filling in a large part of this inlet and using it as part of a through highway around the waterfront of Nanaimo. I would urge the minister to look at this project very carefully before giving his consent to any such filling in of navigable waters.
This small harbour could, if properly handled, be not only an extremely useful small boat harbour on the east coast of Vancouver island, but it could also be an extremely pleasant spot there right at the edge of the city of Nanaimo. It comes right up close to the main street of the city. Properly .developed, it could become a very pleasant .and useful adjunct to that area. It will require, however, to have some dredging of mud; not natural mud but mud that was dumped there many years ago when some building was going on in the city of Nanaimo, when much of it was filled in. There have been a number of illegal fillings in that little inlet, which have been got away with because no one has made a proper formal complaint about them.
I should like to urge the minister to have his department investigate quite thoroughly just what is going on with regard to Commercial inlet in Nanaimo and what plans may have been produced. I have had some sketches sent to me of what is proposed to be done but I have not found out whether or .not it is something that has been approved by the federal government-I do not think it ;has-or whether it is some purely local business firm's scheme. However, it is certainly something that should be looked into before we have the destruction of that little inlet, the complete destruction of something that could be very valuable in that part of the Island. These are matters that I hope the minister and his officials will take under consideration in the very near future.
Just before I sit down, I want to urge the utmost speed in the extension of the dock at Nanaimo because it is very badly needed indeed. I believe the minister himself

observed the crowded condition of the present dock when he was there. If he had been there at any other time he would have seen also the crowded condition of the roadstead, with the deep-sea vessels waiting, sometimes for four or five days, to get into that dock.

I should like to ask the minister for some information with regard to certain matters, or perhaps I should say his views on a certain matter. I think my inquiry can properly be made under the present item. It relates to the proposal for reestablishment of a ferry service across Minas basin in the province of Nova Scotia. I think the minister has a considerable knowledge about the proposal.
Going back a little, I might say that there was a ferry service across there previous to the early 1940's. It was operated by the Dominion Atlantic Railway, a subsidiary of the C.P.R., with the assistance of a comparatively small subsidy, later discontinued, from the federal government. At that time the ferry operated between three ports, Wolf-ville and Kingsport on the southern side of the basin, and Parrsboro, in my constituency, on the northern side of the basin. At each one of these ports there was a wharf which, in addition to being used by the ferry, was used for general wharfage purposes. The subsidy, as I say, was discontinued in the early war years, and consequently the ferry service was discontinued. There is now a strong movement on foot, both in my constituency on the northerly side of the basin and in the Annapolis valley region on the southerly side, for the re-establishment of a ferry service.
Under the old service the ferry could operate only at the top of the tide, and the tide there has a rise and fall of some 30 feet. It is felt that under present conditions a ferry which could operate only once a day would not be adequate and would not by any means fill the need that exists. It has therefore been proposed that a shorter route be established between West Bay, which is just outside Parrsboro, across to a spot called White Waters, which is near famous cape Blomidon on the other side of the bay. Perhaps I should say it is really the Minas channel. The distance is approximately 7 miles, and the ferry could probably shuttle back and forth at intervals of two hours. However, in order to do so it would be necessary to have terminals extending out far enough to afford deep water at all stages of the tide. As the minister knows, a fairly strong movement is afoot of late for the re-establishment of this service.
Of course, the two termini that are now suggested are in the province of Nova Scotia. The ferry does not fall within the category of an interprovincial ferry or one operating

between Canada and some other country. Therefore, of course, certain questions of jurisdiction arise. The cost of the terminals would undoubtedly be very considerable. I believe there have been some estimates made, and they run as high as $2 million.
It should be pointed out, of course, that if these terminals were constructed they would also serve the purpose of general wharfage for general shipping. I should like to ask the minister, in view of the fact that this ferry would be operating between two provincial points; yet having in mind, of course, the fact that these wharves could be used for general purposes; and having in mind also the fact, which I think is true, that such a ferry would be of very great service to both the areas on the north side of the basin and those on the south side, would the minister give us his views briefly with regard to possible federal participation in such a project, particularly with regard to possible participation in the cost of building these terminals?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
I am well aware of the interest of the hon. member for Cumberland in this project. In fact I think he has been one of those who has endeavoured to co-ordinate the actions of other people who are interested in restoring the service that was at one time provided by that ferry, namely the Kipawo, which was discontinued during the war.
The situation is as the hon. member has stated it; that is, it is an intraprovincial operation, and therefore the federal government's interest is not a prior one. The tides in that part of the country are very extreme, and to build wharves that would enable this ferry to operate at any time of the day on a regular schedule would be very expensive indeed, running to something of the order of $2 million, as the hon. member has suggested.
I understand that the particular ferry the local citizens have in mind could be had for something of the order of $60,000, and that they are contemplating a subsidy from the federal government to operate it economically. The federal government normally tries to consider projects of this nature in the light of an investment from which there is some prospect of having a return flow to the taxpayers of the country.
The committees that have been formed have written me on various occasions. In each instance I have asked them if the provincial government has indicated that it is prepared to sponsor such a project and to what extent it is prepared to participate in it. I have stated my views as well as the position the federal government must take in the light of the fact that this would be an intraprovincial ferry. I have not heard the
Supply-Public Works
views of the provincial government expressed, nor have I any idea of the extent to which it is prepared to go into a project of this nature. I am afraid that until we do, and until we have had some request made of us through some official channel by the provincial government, we cannot contemplate undertaking expenditures of the order of magnitude involved.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY

I should just like to add a few words, perhaps by way of advice to the minister and his department. I respectfully suggest that the minister and his department should reappraise their policy with respect to breakwaters along our coast. Two or three years ago there began at Lorneville the construction of a small breakwater which was to greatly benefit the fishermen. But through a tragedy of errors-lack of co-operation between the engineers of the department and private engineers, lack of acceptance of advice in the area, and various other reasons-there grew what we know down that way as the fiasco at Lorneville.
I have been all through this matter with the minister and I do not wish to carry on any further with it, except to say that now in the new breakwater or the new work that is being carried on at Negro point we fear- and a great many people around that area are of the same opinion-that we are getting into the same piecemeal, broken-up mess. They come along with their plans for this breakwater. They add a few more rocks and a little bit is carried on further. I do not know for certain whether the engineering department are in with definite plans in this respect.
I suggest to the minister that there is definite need for a policy with respect to these breakwaters. The minister and his department should decide-I have no quarrel with where the decision to build those breakwaters should come from-the ones that are necessary in order of importance, stick by their decision and carry through in an efficient manner and build them. Otherwise I can say without any fear of contradiction that there is a complete lack of confidence in the policy of the department with respect to these important wharves and breakwaters that are necessary to our fishermen. I merely leave that suggestion with the minister and his department. I may have something to say on particular items later, where I think the minister will probably agree many of these matters should be brought up.

build the breakwater to take the place of the natural breakwater which was by error blown up and destroyed.

speechtext: The next phase, as I mentioned this morning and could have said again but omitted to do so, is that we have at the moment set up a scale model of this harbour at the national research council. It is just about ready for operation now. The machine that simulates the waves has just been calibrated. We hope that by the middle of summer we will have more information, and based thereon we will be able to judge whether further dredging or further improvements are needed beyond this breakwater which is in a well advanced stage of construction right now.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY

speechtext:

speechtext:
I, like my colleague the hon. member for Broadview, am quite surprised to hear the minister say that nothing that can be described as the clearing away of a natural breakwater has taken place. I am not setting myself up as a harbour engineer but I have been several times to Port aux Basques, and my recollection is of going out a fairly long, narrow channel.
I take it also that the minister is aware that there was a conference on this matter last September among the various departments, the Department of Transport, the Department of Public works, experts from the Canadian National Railways and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I must say a press report of that conference does not seem to bear out exactly the description of the situation which the minister has just given us. The press report, which I find at page 2238 of Hansard tor March 16, 1956, said this:
Great was the satisfaction of the ministers that the British expert had confirmed their belief that the dredging operations at Port aux Basques had not ruined the harbour.
That does not seem to speak very well for what has been done. I repeat, I am not going to set myself up as a harbour expert, but again I am expressing tremendous surprise at what the minister has said.
The second thing I want to mention is this. Having regard to the present situation, I mean if you consider the situation of the Bluenose and the Carson at the moment-the Bluenose apparently gets into trouble by rubbing off its propellors on the wharf at Yarmouth, and the Carson finds that she cannot lie quietly enough at the berth at Port aux Basques-I was somewhat disappointed in what the minister said this morning. He said, as I recall, that there was to be a breakwater some 600 feet long. Then he described the model which was at the national research council and upon which I gather experiments were being conducted with a view to seeing what further structural efforts were necessary in order to give the required protection.
Again let me ask the minister, is this breakwater being built in some entirely new place? Am I to understand that nothing has

been done to remove any natural protection which the harbour had? I am confident that has been stated in the house, but I am not able to put my finger on it at the moment. It is very unfortunate the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings is not here. He knows so much more about it than the rest of us. I put that question again. What does the minister say regarding this reference, which certainly does not sound as if everyone were happy about what happened-I shall read it again-
. . . that the dredging operations at Port aux Basques had not ruined the harbour.
As I understand it, the minister goes much further and says there were no dredging operations which in any way injured the harbour. Is that correct?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: I do not want to make a play on words.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: I do not, either.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: I do not want to give any impression that I am saying one thing and meaning another. If I remember correctly, it was I who assembled the meeting to which the hon. member referred; therefore I am pretty well aware of what went on at it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: What was the occasion for holding the meeting?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: To get all the parties together to determine what action should be taken to provide the further protection needed to make this harbour the sort of harbour into which the Canadian National Railways would wish to operate their boat under all conditions of weather and on schedule.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Had there been a previous conference of that kind?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Previous to what?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Previous to the meeting of those parties.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: There had been discussions prior to that, yes. What is the hon. member getting at?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Well, I am getting at this. The project had been under way for, I suppose, a good many months, perhaps some years. I presume there had been conferences before; in fact, I think a year ago we were told there had been. I believe at that time there was a discussion as to where the responsibility really lay as between departments and as between the outside experts who, I think, had been consulted at that time. I would like to ask the minister where the responsibility really lay and what was the situation which the people assembled at that conference were to meet. Was it a situation
Supply-Public Works
of unexpected failure, or was it merely the development of a plan which had reached a certain stage that needed further discussion?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
The situation we were required to meet, or the situation that faced us at that time, was this. Here was this ship that was intended to operate into Port aux Basques. The Canadian National Railways officials said they did not wish to operate the ship into that port because they were not satisfied that under all conditions of weather they could do so safely and meet their schedule. So we met to decide what further action should be taken to make it the sort of harbour they wished to have. We were dealing with something in the future, and we evolved this plan of action.
There seems to be the impression here that this breakwater is being built to replace something that was removed. That is not the case at all. This breakwater is built in an entirely different place at the mouth of Port aux Basques harbour. It is intended to protect the harbour of Port aux Basques, to give some further protection that has never been there before. My hon. friend asked whether the dredging that has been done has ruined the harbour. I say in reply to him again that the report of the experts retained to give us an opinion and to suggest what should be done said that in their opinion the dredging that was done had no appreciable effect on the condition of the harbour, and that is my own view.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: That, of course, is a very conservative statement as compared with what I read from the press. The press said that the British expert had only gone as far as to say the dredging operation at Port aux Basques had not ruined the harbour. Perhaps this discussion should be set aside until we have seen the report to which the minister referred. Could we have that report?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: It was a report to the Minister of Transport. Perhaps the hon. member could ask him.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: He is not in his place. Can we get the report before this item is finished?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: I am not going to undertake to table a report prepared for the Minister of Transport; no.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: One last question, Mr. Chairman; in preparing this harbour was any island or were any reefs, or anything of that kind, which protected the harbour in any way, destroyed?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: My hon. friend is trying to prove in some way or other-

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Trying to get some information.

Supply-Public Works

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Yes, but for the purpose of proving that something was done that has destroyed the value of this harbour. There was dredging done in the harbour. A channel was dredged from the outer harbour into this new dock that was built. Rock was removed when the channel was dredged. It was all below water. No surface rock was removed to my knowledge, and I think I am correct in saying that. The engineers confirm that I am correct in saying that. To that is added the statement of the English firm of consultants, and my own view, that none of that dredging had any significant effect on the harbour at all.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a representative of one of the smaller but main municipalities in the best riding in the dominion, I should like to say 1 am very glad that the minister and his deputy are widely travelled men. We should be looking forward to their improving their knowledge and education by visiting our county of Bruce some time in the near future. In the opinion of some we are small, but we have a wonderful county. We expect that our population will increase greatly in the next two decades.
Because the population of the county is going to grow by leaps and bounds many of the larger municipalities are having difficulties in various ways and some of them are beginning to call for help from outside their own municipalities. If there are such conditions in those municipalities we should smarten up and not try to grow any more. It seems to me that it has been very hard to do anything about decentralization. I shall not use Mark Twain's remark which has been often quoted.
This federal government have been delinquent in doing anything about it. They are not the only government that have been delinquent. Some provincial governments have also been delinquent. In fact at the present time I am sorry to say that one of our provincial governments has brought in legislation having to do with piping water from localities which are ideal for industrial purposes into larger inland centres. If those centres remained at their present size they would be better places for the labouring people to live in than if they became larger. If it ever happened that any government has to pay subsidies on such work I for one would strongly oppose it.
In Bruce county we have, as I said recently, a great shore line, and we are looking forward to an increasing population. Kincardine has been negotiating with the Department of Public Works for over 30 years for a proper harbour. In my opinion the present Minister of Public Works and his deputy are astute
[Mr. Hees.l
businessmen. I do not believe they take a political view in any of their decisions and, therefore, I believe we shall obtain some satisfaction in the future when the minister and his deputy realize that the people in Bruce are very sincere. If we were not sincere we would not have petitioned this government for over 30 years for a harbour at Kincardine. If we were not sincere the Department of Public Works would not have such a large file on the matter, which even includes plans that have been drawn on three different occasions.
With the deep waterway being constructed at the present time, if the minister will give this serious thought I think he will find that Kincardine is a logical place for a haven harbour to be built. Estimates have been made as to the cost of the harbour, and the actual cost could be more or less than what is estimated. Foresight will have to be exercised in the spending of large amounts of money.
I would suggest that within the next 12 months the department and its advisers should concentrate very thoroughly on the matter of locating a haven harbour at Kincardine to handle the increased shipping on the great lakes. This is not a local project only, because it concerns people who live within a radius of a great many miles in this very fertile district. If this request is not acted upon within the next short while it may be too late.
I think the minister would do well to have a talk with the chairman of the Gordon commission; he could probably get some advice from Mr. Gordon. If the minister were to seek advice I am satisfied that it would be along the lines of the advice I am giving him at the present time.
I understand that the department's plan of administration is not to spend any money except for commercial purposes. On the peninsula there are many small communities whose only commercial line is the tourist trade. Many of these people need a few dollars spent there to facilitate the handling of those tourists who come to stay for the summer. I would ask the department to look into that matter and to consider the fact that the tourist business is the whole commercial life of a great many of the people of the peninsula. By spending a few dollars there the ability of the local inhabitants to earn a livelihood will be increased.
In concluding my remarks I wish to point out that the Department of Public Works has cut down its expenditure this year. Perhaps the minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I think it has been cut by between $5 million and $6 million; am I right?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Approximately 50 per cent of the amount of that decrease is made in the items for harbours and rivers in Ontario. If the same thing should occur next year perhaps the minister will consider spending approximately $2,500,000 on the construction of the harbour at Kincardine. If he and his officials were to do this, I am sure they would go down in history as being farsighted, and perhaps their action would justify the erection of one of the plaques which we heard criticized this morning.
