maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, returning to the matter of Toronto harbour, which was touched upon by the hon. members for Scarborough and York West, I might say that some two years ago I asked the minister to investigate the erosion on that part of lake Ontario which is in Danforth riding. He said at that time that no consideration could be given to it unless it had to do with navigation; that to be considered a matter must constitute a danger or peril to navigation.
The hon. member for Scarborough has spoken about the difficulty which comes about as a result of the Scarborough bluffs. He made some reference to the bluffs going out and said he was probably the only bluff left. Perhaps I could correct that statement for him by saying that he is not the big bluff he thinks he is but he belongs to a party which is the biggest bluff.
To get back to the problem in the Toronto area, however, the hon. member brought out the fact that the old area that was in the city of Toronto proper, governed and controlled by the Toronto harbour board, is going through a period of transition. Toronto has had added to it Scarborough, New Toronto, Long Branch, Mimico and Etobicoke. In other words it embraces the area from the Etobicoke river to Rouge river, and is now known as metropolitan Toronto.
With regard to the problem of navigation, I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the sand and other material coming from Scarborough Bluffs constantly creates ledges and bars or fills up the eastern gap and thus constitutes a danger to navigation. Considerable dredging will have to be done. The hon. member for York-Scarborough said there would have to be some enlargement or some revision of the Toronto harbour board in order to administer the area which has been mentioned. The period of transition is the time to bring up these matters, as it should take some considerable time to effect this change.
I think the department should give some consideration to the shore line of lake Ontario. Expenditures are made by the Toronto harbour board, on which this government has a representative, but they pertain only to

Supply-Public Works
repair work and dredging with the perimeter of the harbour, which includes Toronto bay and what is left of old Ashbridge's bay in which there are three or four turning basins. The shore line of lake Ontario running from highway No. 27 or beginning at Long Branch to the eastern limits of Scarborough would be approximately 30 miles, and very little attention has been given to it. Serious attention must be given to that particular shore line running from Fallingbrook avenue to Cherry street or the eastern gap. Lifeguard service in this area is augmented by voluntary organizations.
The hon. member for Greenwood will remember the cut which used to run from Ashbridge's bay to the lake, but this area has been filled in by the Toronto harbour commission. More serious consideration will have to be given to this particular shore line with the building of the new seaway. As the hon. member for York-Scarborough has mentioned, the Rouge river at Port Union should provide harbour facilities and a haven from storms, and the old Ashbridge's bay cut should also be used for that purpose.
Representations have been made to me to have something done about the old Ashbridge's bay cut being made into a haven and brought into operation. The Toronto harbour board should be approached so the necessary cooperation can be obtained. This is part of their job, to look after this area, and at the proper time we will make representations to the government through the harbour board.
As the hon. member for York-Scarborough has said, something will have to be done immediately with regard to that portion of the shore to which he referred. Every time here is a slide at Scarborough Bluffs more sand and silt is pushed into lake Ontario and then is carried by lake currents into the eastern harbour and in time creates sand bars and ledges. Such silt gathering there becomes an impediment to navigation in lake Ontario.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure sufficient has been said in this chamber to acquaint hon. members with the fact that the mighty Fraser in British Columbia is not only a great boon to us but also brings to us a number of very vital problems. I have referred to this matter on other occasions, especially with regard to the erosion problem which we have in Fraser Valley constituency. At the present time I am thinking of the matter more from the standpoint of navigation in the section of the river below the village of Hope.
In many of these sections the river, instead of being confined to one channel, is finding its way into other channels, while in other

sections it is cutting back until it is running almost at right angles to the normal direction of the flow. It would seem to us that a long-range plan to confine the river to one channel should be developed, such plan to be realized by dredging and by filling in or blocking undesirable sloughs and channels that are to be found in some sections of the river. I submit that some effort should be made to straighten out some of the bad points in the river. We realize that this would involve a considerable amount of work under an overall plan, but when we consider the work being done just to take care of emergency situations I think it would be advisable to work out some over-all plan for the solution of the problem.
The particular section of the Fraser river to which I have referred is used to a considerable extent by tug boats towing log booms from logging camps in the Fraser canyon, in the upper Fraser valley and in the Harrison lake area. A considerable volume of scow traffic is carried into and out of Harrison lake on the Fraser and Harrison rivers, having to do mostly with construction work and the carriage of logging machinery and supplies. There is also some movement of heavy equipment up to Rosedale and Hope.
According to the information I have, during the past year 130 million board feet of logs were towed from Harrison lake down to Harrison river, into the Fraser just opposite Chilliwack, and then down the Fraser to the lower mainland area. From the Hope area and the Fraser canyon there were 70 million feet of logs towed from about 14 different logging camps. About 10 million feet of those were bundled logs from the canyon, and it is expected that when this particular type of operation has been proved it will be used to a much greater extent.
The future use of the river is of vital concern. Already a number of companies have indicated their interest in the use of the river for the transportation of manufactured products. Inquiries have been received from companies which already have plants in existence, while in other cases new plants would be established if transportation by barge were available or could be carried on in this section. With the trend toward the greater utilization of wood products, local manufacturers in that area are at a serious disadvantage in not being able to have a market for chips and other salvaged wood products because of the high transportation costs. I have a list of the companies which are interested in using the river for transportation purposes.

There are a number of sections in this river which constitute trouble spots. When I refer to the dredging of the Fraser river I am not referring to the entire length of the river from Hope down to the sea. The river bottom is a series of deep holes and shallow spots, and the channels are created where the shallow spots occur.
I could give a list this afternoon of some of those trouble spots, but I do not think it would be necessary or of particular value to us at the moment to discuss them. I would just point out that the Cheam area on the C.N.R. is one of the most difficult and most important spots. Here the river makes a right angle bend and is still*cutting back into what will eventually be, if the process continues, an S-turn. In this particular instance it may have more to do with flood prevention than with actual transport problems. So I just call this to the attention of the minister to indicate that there are certain sections of the river that we feel should be attended to, in order not only to take care of erosion problems but also to facilitate the transportation of products down the river.
I would also call attention to the fact that in the neighbourhood of the new Rosedale bridge a serious problem obtains, in that there is a bad cross current that makes it extremely difficult to tow the logs between the piers of that bridge. At the present time I understand there are two barges employed on the Fraser and Harrison rivers in the Hope area and below Hope. The Fraser River Dredging Company is using a river bulldozer, and the Scuffler Dredge Company is using a drag bucket.
I am given to understand that last year representations were made to the federal Department of Public Works in Vancouver over the fact that the dredging equipment was occupied in the Harrison river during the early fall, when possibly it could have been used to greater advantage in the Fraser. The thought has been expressed that dredging in the Harrison river could and should be done in the spring and early summer, leaving the equipment for use in the Fraser at a time when it would be more effective; that is, in the early fall and winter. At that time the department stated that moneys were not appropriated early enough in the year to make an early start possible in the Harrison. This is very important as far as my particular riding is concerned, and not only my riding but, of course, all the industries that are located in that section and those in the lower mainland area that obtain their supplies of products from up the river.
Last fall I spent some time in going around looking over the various river problems with
Supply-Public Works
different delegations. My attention was directed to a situation in the Matsqui prairie area, where river bank erosion is still causing a very serious condition. It is expected that if it is not remedied it will not be very long before the dikes themselves will be in danger from the action of erosion. The situation at Albion has been brought to the attention of the minister on a number of occasions, but mostly in connection with requests for river bank protection work, but here again it has been suggested that river dredging would possibly be a solution to the problem. The end of, I believe, McMillan island has been cut off by the action of the current, and now the current is being directed right across the river to the north side, where it is causing severe erosion problems.
I think the consensus of opinion is that the only satisfactory solution to the problem in this whole area is a channeling program. In fact that view has been expressed on quite a number of occasions at great length. So we would request that when the minister and his department are considering all these different problems and working out their different projects, they give consideration to a survey of that whole section with a view to working out a long-term program, or I should say an extensive program, that would take care of this situation, assist in the prevention of flood conditions and also provide transportation facilities on the Fraser river from Hope down to the sea.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 167, to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move second reading of this bill I wish to explain immediately its purpose. The purpose is set out in the explanatory note, which reads as follows:
The object of this bill is to provide that when a fine is imposed under the summary convictions provisions of the Criminal Code (part XXIV), there shall be mandatory action taken by the court to assure, subject to certain reservations,-
To prevent any unfairness of any improprieties taking place.
-that a warrant of commitment shall not issue for imprisonment forthwith of the person on whom the fine has been imposed, because of financial inability to make immediate payment.
The bill consists of amendments to the Criminal Code which was amended some

years ago, in particular section 694. Section 694 reads as follows:
694. (1) Except where otherwise expressly provided by law, every one who is convicted of an offence punishable on summary conviction is liable to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars or to imprisonment for six months or to both.
And subsection 2:
(2)	Where the imposition of a fine or the making of an order for the payment of money is authorized by law, but the law does not provide that imprisonment may be imposed in default of payment of the fine or compliance with the order, the court may order that in default of payment of the fine or compliance with the order, as the case may be, the defendant shall be imprisoned for a period of not more than six months.
*
Over the years I have belonged to that group of people who believe that our law in respect of the imposition of imprisonment in lieu of the payment of a fine is not only antiquated but is also unjust. When the amendments to the Criminal Code came before the house I endeavoured to convince hon. members-and on a number of occasions I have argued in favour of such an amendment -of the need for an amendment which would provide that instead of a person being summarily liable to imprisonment because of his inability to pay a fine, an investigation should take place into his financial position, and that imprisonment should not be arbitrarily and mandatorily imposed. When the matter was discussed during general discussion on the amendments to the Criminal Code some years ago an amendment was agreed to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) which was to the following effect:
(3)	A summary conviction court may direct that any fine, pecuniary penalty or sum of money adjudged to be paid shall be paid forthwith or, if the accused is unable to pay forthwith, at such time and on such terms as the summary conviction court may fix.
That section as amended has not generally been acted upon. It is not mandatory. Many a man is sentenced to imprisonment today in default of a fine simply because of the fact that his financial position makes it impossible for him to pay his fine, or his poverty prevents him being able to do so. The purpose of the amendment is to make it mandatory, having regard to the action of the court-subject to the reservations I shall mention-that a person shall not be imprisoned in the event that he is unable to pay his fine but that an investigation shall take place on the part of the magistrate and in that case time shall be granted to enable that person to pay his fine, either by instalments or otherwise.
I start by making the general admission that, as is known by Your Honour and by members of the legal profession, there are

many magistrates who grant extensions within the meaning of the new section which was brought into effect some two or three years ago. But those who actually grant extensions are in the minority. It is much easier-and much less difficult and trying administratively -when a fine of $5 and costs is imposed, if immediate imprisonment be ordered than if an extension be granted within which the individual may make payment of the fine and costs.
During the years I have practised law, during which I have handled a large number of defences and a considerable number of prosecutions, I have seen-as I think have members of the bar generally-too many cases in which decent, respectable persons whose only fault is their poverty, find themselves unable to pay a fine and are then incarcerated in prison in default of payment. Whether that prison term be 10 days or 30 days, the individual who cannot pay his fine is stigmatized for the balance of his life. No matter what that individual may subsequently endeavour to do in order to erase that term of imprisonment, ever and anon it makes its appearance.
Indeed, since I introduced this bill on first reading, I have had a number of letters from persons across Canada whose only offence was a petty one for which a fine was a reasonable and suitable punishment. However, because of their inability to pay that fine they have suffered terms of imprisonment and have subsequently found themselves detrimentally affected in consequence of that period of imprisonment. On many occasions I have been shocked to see coming before the courts men who have committed offences which any of us might have committed-petty offences such as breaches of municipal laws, traffic offences and the like-and whose inability to pay the fines has meant imprisonment and forever the mark of Cain in consequence of that imprisonment.
I doubt whether there are many Canadians who realize the march to the jails taking place in our country, in a considerable measure due to the fact that we still maintain imprisonment as a mandatory alternative to the payment of a fine except within the limitation mentioned a few moments ago, when I set' out the power that exists in the court to direct a payment on terms. It is there in the book, but it is seldom used.
How many of us realize the extent of this march to the jails within Canada? The figures are not up to date. What I have before me is the Canada Year Book for 1955, and that tells the story. In 1952 the number of persons admitted to penal institutions in Canada
Criminal Code
amounted to 99,163. In 1951 it amounted to
99,062. The number is now over 100,000 a year. Most of the offences of these people are offences punishable by jail sentences, but the turnover is indicated by these statistics. In 1952, 87,917 were admitted to common jails and 87,763 were discharged. In other words, the large proportion of the 100,000 Canadians who go to jail every year spend a comparatively short time there. The figures in 1951 were approximately the same.
Why is this? Why is it that our jails are loaded down as the penal institutions of few other countries are? Compare our situation with Great Britain. Making all the allowances that are often made, why is it that in proportion to population we have three and a half times as many people in our penal institutions as has Great Britain? Well, one of the reasons, and the major reason, is the fact that more than 40 years ago in Great Britain they abolished this system of mandatory imprisonment for non-payment of fines. In this country, in our administration of criminal justice for minor offences, we are 50 years behind the times, although the situation revealed by the Williams case indicates that red tape and faulty administration play too important a part in the administration of justice. In so far as minor offences are concerned, no serious change has been made in the Criminal Code in more than 50 years.
Why have not the advances in modern penological experience been incorporated within our laws to the extent they should? Only recently a great speech was made on this subject in another place by a former member of this house. He set out the very serious degree to which in the administration of our criminal jurisprudence, rehabilitation of the individual plays so small a part that recidivism claims some 76 per cent of all those who at one time or another receive prison sentences. When an individual receives a prison sentence for his inability to pay a fine, too often that is the first step along the road leading to recidivism and the almost continued occupancy of a cell.
Why is it that knowing the benefits that have accrued from the operation of the law in Great Britain, passed as I said 42 years ago, a similar amendment to our law has not been brought into effect? In Britain this matter came before the House of Commons in April, 1914. I am not going to read the debates. They are to be found in English Hansard for April 15, 1914, and in subsequent volumes. This provision became law on August 10, 1914, just after Britain entered the first war. Read the list of those who spoke in the British House of Commons. It is almost a Who's Who of subsequently great

Criminal Code
people in the annals of Great Britain. There were some, however, who used the same arguments in opposition to this amendment as I have seen referred to in the press. One is that if imprisonment in default of a fine were removed it would be an encouragement to those who are poor to commit crimes. Another argument is that it would increase the number of crimes; that the poor would have an incentive.
It is said that there are circumstances under which there should be no extension of time for the payment of a fine, and I can envisage some of those circumstances. In order to cover those circumstances I have placed in part of the amendment words which will give to the court the right, for any special reason, to deny to the individual any extension of time. One of those reasons may be the nature of the offence. It may be that the individual is a repeater or it may be that for some other good and sufficient reason the fine should be paid forthwith, regardless of any excuses advanced by the individual. In those cases the magistrate shall have that power, but shall be required to note upon the warrant of commitment the reason an extension of time for payment was not granted by the court.
I mentioned a moment ago that one of the reasons there has been little change in the number of cases in which an extension of time has been granted as a result of the amendment of two years ago is that it is not mandatory that there be an investigation. It is purely a voluntary section giving to the court the right to grant an extension if and when it feels like doing so. What did Britain find in 1912, the last year in respect of which statistics were available? There were 80,000 British people who went to jail because of their inability to pay fines. The bill was introduced by the secretary of state for the home department, Mr. Reginald McKenna, and he pointed out that of the 80,000 who were committed about 13,000 paid their fines in whole or in part after commitment, and the rest were imprisoned until the conclusion of their sentences. He and others associated with him pointed out the injustice inherent in imprisonment because of poverty.
Among those who participated in the debate, sir, were some men who subsequently attained greatness: Sir William Anson, a name to conjure with in the legal world; Samuel Hoare; Joynson-Hicks; Robert Har-court; Hamer Greenwood, and others. Then, when you come to the vote, sir, on July 20, 1914, among those who voted on that occasion-and apparently it was not a party vote- were Sir John Simon; Sir Stanley Buck-master; Augustine Birrell; H. H. Asquith; Stanley Baldwin; and Ramsay MacDonald.

All these men were at the time either nationally or internationally known. All subsequently became such, and every one of them supported the amendment of 1914.
That amendment to the law is to be found in "Public General Acts, 1914", chapter 58. In general that has been the law since 1914. The change that came about when it was brought into being was a very marked reduction in the jail population of Great Britain, which has continued to be the case ever since in respect of minor offences. The amendment which I move is in large measure incorporated in the act of 1914, changed only in certain particulars which the British people found necessary to change on the basis of their experience.
Finally a further act was passed in 1935, called the money payments act, which is to be found in the 14th volume of Halsbury's Statutes of England, second edition. Ever since the British people changed the law in this regard it is specific in so far as offenders under 21 years are concerned. They cannot be imprisoned because of their inability to pay a fine. Go to our jails and penal institutions, sir, and see something of the change that has taken place in recent years. See the number of young offenders, many of them there because of offences for which a fine was a fair and reasonable penalty. Since they were unable to pay the fine they had to suffer the penalty of imprisonment and a lifetime stigma that no future good conduct can eradicate.
I endeavoured to secure the statistics for Canada. I wrote to the various attorneys general of the provinces to find out how many persons in the jails of each of the provinces during the period of five years were imprisoned because of the inability of the offender to pay a fine. Interestingly enough, outside of two provinces none of the attorneys general or their staffs had any available data on the subject. The province of Ontario had a composite picture, but not complete in itself. The only province that had a picture approximately correct was the province of Quebec. The attorney general wrote me on April 7 and said this:
It is impossible to supply you with the exact figures. However, I have had a quick study made, in order to give you approximate numbers. The results are as follows:

approximately	2,825
I want publicly to pay my tribute to the deputy attorney general of Quebec for furnishing that very important information, in which is clearly indicated the degree of

seriousness inherent in the imposition of fines which the individual cannot pay.
On the face of it I cannot see any serious argument that can be advanced against this bill. It has been weighed in the scales of experience in Britain. Similar legislation has been passed in a number of states of the American union. The statistics reveal that, whether in consequence of the change of the law or not, the number of young offenders has been greatly reduced wherever a similar law, or an analogous one, is in effect. Why should we not in this House of Commons, without regard to party consideration, try this plan, give it a trial for a year or two? Something must be done to meet the accelerating degree to which our young men are finding themselves in prison and, following their release, again returned to prison. Imprisonment, because of the failure to pay a fine, causes resentment in the heart of the individual upon whom that fine is imposed that is not easily erased.
I have on my desk a letter from a man in Toronto who tells his story. It could be multiplied and is multiplied to the knowledge of lawyers in every part of the house. In August this man received an increase of $3 a week in salary. It was a Saturday. He became intoxicated and was picked up by the police. It was not until Tuesday that sufficient money was raised to pay the remainder of his fine, then unexpiated and unearned. He lost his job, and whenever he has made an application for a position since he has been faced with the fact that imprisonment came to him under those circumstances eight or nine months ago.
The British people have found in their experience that the amendments of 1914 have paid tremendous returns in good citizenship. I do not know why it is, but I sometimes feel that in the field of criminal law and procedure we in this nation are far behind the advances made in other nations with similar backgrounds and traditions.
We had the Archambault report. It made many recommendations, some of which have been implemented. At the present time a commission is sitting which indeed may have already made a report. This commission is composed of distinguished jurists and lawyers. I do not endeavour to anticipate what that report will be, but I do say that anyone with any knowledge of our criminal courts knows that too often our measures of punishment are indeed measures that open the portals of a life to almost permanent wrongdoing.
I mentioned the Williams case, which is a tragic example of the kind of mentality that
Criminal Code
exists. Here a man 20 years of age, never before having committed any crime, commits a series of crimes within a period of six weeks and is imprisoned for 28 years. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice spoke of the means being taken to rehabilitate him. He has been in prison now for five years; yet when a nationally known magazine such as Maclean's sets out the facts, undenied and undeniable as they are, the processes of our administration deny the application of ordinary principles of justice.
We did not have any difficulty, sir, in finding a means whereby the views of the Supreme Court of Canada could be ascertained in the Coffin case. The means used was an order in council under the Supreme Court Act. By no stretch of the imagination was an order in council ever conceived to be the means whereby the Supreme Court of Canada could receive the power to do that for which it did not possess the power. If it could be done in the Coffin case, could it not also have been done in the Williams case?
If the present Penitentiaries Act and the Ticket of Leave Act and the law respecting parole cannot be applied in the Williams case, is this not the type of case in which action could be taken to submit to the court the question as to whether or not the infamy of a 28-year sentence, so unreasonable and dissimilar from that imposed in other cases, is in keeping with the highest traditions of justice within our country?
I am shocked when I read the record of the Williams case and compare it with the case of another young man 26 years of age who went on a crime rampage and staged six armed hold-ups. The second young man was able to secure the services of an eminent counsel, and he received a sentence of six years' imprisonment. The Minister of Justice says nothing can be done about the Williams case, but that it is receiving consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I was
merely illustrating by an outstanding current example something of the rigidity that characterizes the administration of our criminal law today. When you say I have cast reflections on the courts, I point out to you that every time a counsel appeals against a sentence by a lower court he always points out the salient errors. Incidentally, when he appeals against a sentence the number one ground is that the sentence given shocks the conscience and for that reason is appealable.
I simply used the Williams case as an example of what I have been trying to point out today, and it is this. Let us try to change our criminal law in those regards which are covered by the purview of the bill before the house to the end that we shall not, because of rigidity in our administration, fail to make those changes in the law which experience in other countries and which common sense would dictate as necessary.
Britain found 42 years ago that 80,000 persons were going to jail each year because of their inability to pay their fines. The law was then changed. Extensions of time for payment are not generally given today, excepting within the restricted area which I mentioned earlier in my argument, and which must be in the law to ensure that no one shall take advantage of the opportunity to commit an offence because he realizes that his poverty will prevent him from going to jail if he fails to pay his fine. Britain found that this change in the law emptied the jails.
We should consider the terrific cost of our jail system in Canada today with eighty-nine or ninety thousand Canadians going into jail each year and approximately the same number being released. My submission is that we in parliament have a responsibility to give serious consideration to the need for legislation like this to be incorporated in our law; for certainly if we preserve only 100 individuals in this country from receiving the stigma of one term in jail, and as a result they are able to pay their fines afterward and are saved from becoming recidivists, this bill will have indeed achieved everything which I am hopeful it will achieve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of justice is too important to any country to be allowed to deteriorate. It is therefore necessary that a country should constantly review its justice, its laws and the procedure of its courts. Bill No. 167 attempts to remove what I believe might be termed a discrimination as between the rich and the poor in the case of summary convictions. I believe it should have and that it will receive the support of all thinking members of this house.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
The principle of this bill is to permit any accused person who is unable to pay a fine imposed, because of his financial position, to be granted a period of time in which to pay that penalty. In modern life it is quite natural that some people shall have wealth while others have not. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Prince Albert, who has introduced this bill, at times it is difficult to obtain immediately the money required, and the result is that the person who is unable to do so finds himself faced with the disgrace of imprisonment. Surely it is wrong that a poorer person should be compelled to suffer the disgrace of a prison term while wealthier citizens are able to escape. The fact that such a thing exists in Canada is not good for Canada's reputation. In the meting out of justice Great Britain has found it advisable to remove this injustice, which indicates that Canada has been a bit slow in bringing about this change in our law.
I do not know of any ground upon which anyone could oppose this bill. Perhaps someone will say that it would be difficult to arrange instalment payments, that this would place the court in the position of a collection agency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make just a few brief remarks on the principle of this bill. It is certainly a bill which any young lawyer would find interest in dissecting. I have no doubt but that this bill springs from the humanitarian impulses which so often motivate the hon. member for Prince Albert. The picture

[DOT]conjured up by the old Dickensian story of imprisonment for debt, when we were told of how Mr. Pickwick and Sam Weller were lodged in jail for not paying money that was owing, is certainly much different from what is the case today. We have advanced far from the days when a person could be imprisoned for a civil debt.
I think probably this bill springs from the situation where a debt is created in the form of a fine imposed by a magistrate. It is a debt to the court which, as has been pointed out, in some cases cannot be paid. In introducing the bill the hon. member for Prince Albert referred to the section under which a magistrate finds his jurisdiction in matters of this kind. If the house will bear with me I should like to refer again to section 694 (3) which reads:
A summary conviction court may direct that any fine, pecuniary penalty or sum of money adjudged to be paid shall be paid forthwith or, if the accused is unable to pay forthwith, at such time and on such terms as the summary conviction court may fix.
I imagine that what the hon. member for Prince Albert objects to in the present law is the use of the word "may" in that section. He would like to have it made arbitrary that the magistrate examine the possibility of time payments rather than the permissive stipulation in the present section. The question, then, is if this change in the section is made and we adopt a bill similar to the one proposed, will it have any practical impact upon the situation. I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member say that he did not think magistrates were very prone to grant extensions of time for the payment of fines, and I think he said that in the majority of cases they did not grant any such extension.
I have not had too wide an experience in matters of this kind, although I have done some work in magistrates' courts. Perhaps because of the short passage of time I have not risen to the exalted heights on which the hon. member for Prince Albert finds himself when appearing in court, but in my short experience I have found that magistrates are often very humane in their outlook. This clause gives them freedom to take all circumstances into account, such as inability to pay and so on. I wonder if it is necessary for them to have that freedom.
I realize that there is a terrific problem in the administration of justice at the magistrate's level, certainly in large metropolitan centres where the magistrate, particularly on Monday morning, is faced with a tremendous number of cases. Anyone who has been present in court at that time will realize the problem. These people come before the magistrate charged with minor offences. There is
Criminal Code
a tremendous number of charges of drunkenness, in many cases a repetition of previous charges. The magistrate and the crown attorney have a list of previous convictions, and in many of these cases the sentence is $5 or five days. Quite often the accused person will just march off, sometimes gladly, to the cell.
I do not know, but it seems to me that the Quebec statistics which the hon. member for Prince Albert quoted must have included a number of cases of that type, where the magistrate would be faced with a tremendously difficult problem. He made a good attempt to obtain figures from the other provinces as to the number who were in prison because of their inability to pay fines, and it is unfortunate that there were not more figures forthcoming. It is rather hard to canvass the situation intelligently and reach any sound judgment unless you know exactly what the situation is in that respect.
There is another point. I think this section certainly should be made more use of if the other officials in the court apart from the magistrate would raise the problem of the inability of the accused to pay the fine. So often in these courts the accused has no one to speak for him. There is no counsel acting on his behalf, and the case is tried very quickly in this log jam of cases that faces the people administering justice in this country. Before the accused knows what has happened the case is finished. Often I feel that other court officials, such as the crown attorneys, could take a little more time perhaps to point out to the accused that it is possible to ask for time in which to pay their fines.

Section 694A of the proposed Bill No. 167 sets out the conditions under which time might be granted. It reads:
A warrant committing a person to prison in respect of non-payment of a fine adjudged to be paid by the court shall not be issued forthwith unless the court which passed the sentence is satisfied that he is possessed of sufficient means to enable him to pay the fine forthwith, or-
Then there are two conditions:
-or unless, upon being asked by the court whether he desires that time should be allowed for payment, he does not express any such desire, or

unless the court for any other special reason expressly desires that no time shall be allowed.
I do not think the member who introduced the bill examined too thoroughly the last phrase in that sentence. This section would give the magistrate a way out of even putting the question. In other words, he need not go into the question if for any special reasons he expressed the desire that no time should be allowed.

It may be that I do not fully understand the wording of the section, but it seemed to me that this condition rather milked the section of any new or practical effect it might have. Obviously, before you adopted such a measure something like that would have to be very carefully gone into. It is interesting to note, in a further examination of the present section of the Criminal Code, a case quoted on page 685 of Snow's Criminal Code of Canada, sixth edition, which is the latest edition. This is the case of Rex v. Mackie (1944). The judge in the case indicated the following:
A fine is payable forthwith but if the accused is unable to pay forthwith the justice or magistrate may direct that the fine be paid at such time and on such terms as he may fix . . .
The statement goes on:
It is always the duty of a court when imposing punishment to take into consideration the circumstances in which the crime has been committed. There is no rule governing a uniform punishment for particular crimes.
It seems to me that the judge in that case was trying to point out that it is always the duty of the court to take into account the ability to pay the fine. Therefore, with any sort of effective representation at all, an accused has the advantage of this law that is already in existence.
Again we run into the old problem of the constitution. If you produce a law here in this house, which is in turn administered by the provincial house, they of course have complete control over the administration of justice in the province. I would submit that
as the law presently stands-and I submit this very respectfully-the province has the power if it wants to tighten up in this particular situation. I submit that it already has the power to do so under the existing law. As has been said, it may be that the administration of justice is too rigid in the province. Perhaps that is something in which many of us can agree.

speechtext: Has the hon. member for York-Scarborough concluded his remarks?

maintopic: QUESTIONS TO BE ASKED ON ORDERS OF THE DAY

Yes, I have concluded.
On motion of Mr. Fulton the debate was adjourned.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we shall start on Monday with the Trans-Canada Highway Act in committee, then take the housing resolution; then second reading of the agreement with respect to income tax with the Kingdom of Denmark; then the resolution in the name of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and then the resolution in my name with respect to the Public Service Superannuation Act.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
